description_full: Ralph Lauren Corporation designs, markets, and distributes lifestyle products in North America, Europe, Asia, and internationally. The company offers apparel, including a range of men's, women's, and children's clothing; footwear and accessories, which comprise casual shoes, dress shoes, boots, sneakers, sandals, eyewear, watches, fashion and fine jewelry, scarves, hats, gloves, and umbrellas, as well as leather goods comprising handbags, luggage, small leather goods, and belts; home products, such as bed and bath lines, furniture, fabric and wall coverings, lighting, dining, floor coverings, decorative accessories, and giftware; and fragrances. The company sells apparel and accessories under the Ralph Lauren Collection, Ralph Lauren Purple Label, Polo Ralph Lauren, Double RL, Lauren Ralph Lauren, RLX Ralph Lauren, Polo Ralph Lauren Children, and Chaps brands; women's fragrances under the Ralph Lauren Collection, Woman by Ralph Lauren, Romance Collection, and Ralph Collection brand names; and men's fragrances under the Ralph's Club, Purple Label, Polo Blue, Polo Red, Polo Green, Polo Black, Polo 67, Safari, Polo Sport, and Big Pony Men's brand names. Its restaurant collection includes The Polo Bar in New York City; RL Restaurant in Chicago; Ralph's in Paris; The Bar at Ralph Lauren located in Milan; Ralph's Bar located in Chengdu, China; and Ralph's Coffee concept. The company sells its products to department stores, specialty stores, and golf and pro shops, as well as directly to consumers through its retail stores, concession-based shop-within-shops, and its digital commerce sites. It operates retail stores and concession-based shop-within-shops; and operates Ralph Lauren stores and shops through licensing partners. Ralph Lauren Corporation was founded in 1967 and is based in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Ralph Lauren Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $22.8B market cap on $8.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 42% against a 10% cost of capital — a 32-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 60% confirm genuine pricing power.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 22× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.6% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 7pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.83x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 1.09, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $208.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 37% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $141 (margin of safety -174%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 40%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 14.9 vs 10.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 72% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $448 on average, 16% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 42% clears the cost of capital of 9.7% by 32pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.63).
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.23x.
ROE of 33% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $826.1M (4% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.0% over 3 years, 13.0% over 5 years and 0.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 16.0% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 3.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (2.7% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 34.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 15,600 employees, each generates about $520K of revenue, 1.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 2.3% a year across its filed history.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $9.6M (18x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
